goal: Traffic light on an Arduino Uno: a red LED on pin D11, a yellow LED on D10 and a green LED on D9, each through a 220 ohm resistor, in a column like a real traffic light, plus a crosswalk push button on D2 (wired to GND, using INPUT_PULLUP) that starts a walk cycle.

plan.title: Arduino traffic light with crosswalk request button
plan.summary: Build a red, yellow and green traffic light controlled by an Arduino Uno. Pressing the crosswalk button changes green to yellow for 2 seconds, then red for a 5-second crossing interval, before returning to green; the red light is the crossing cue, with no separate walk LED.
plan.final_result: The LEDs form one evenly spaced line: red at row 10, yellow at row 20 and green at row 30. With row 1 facing upward, they appear in a vertical traffic-light column. Once the sketch is loaded and USB power is present, only green lights initially. A button press gives 2 seconds of yellow, then 5 seconds of red as the crossing cue, then green again. Presses during a cycle are ignored; release and press again after green returns to request another cycle.
safety: Keep the Uno disconnected from USB and other power while inserting or changing components.
Use USB power for this project; do not connect mains electricity or a 12 V supply to breadboard holes or Arduino GPIO pins.
Each LED must retain its own 220 ohm series resistor. Never replace a resistor with a jumper.
Keep exposed LED and resistor leads from touching adjacent leads, and never force the button into incompatible holes.
The button needs no external pull-up resistor because the sketch enables INPUT_PULLUP. Do not connect the button to 5 V.
This is a tabletop demonstration, not a real road or pedestrian safety controller.

part_guide.breadboard: The white board with numbered rows holds the circuit without solder. Holes a through e in one row connect together; f through j form a separate group.
part_guide.uno: The Arduino Uno is the controller board with USB and labelled headers. It runs the traffic-light timing and reads the button.
part_guide.led_red: The red round LED shows stop during the crossing interval. Its long leg is the anode (+); its short leg beside the flat rim is the cathode (-).
part_guide.res_red: This small banded 220 ohm resistor limits the red LED's current. A common four-band marking is red-red-brown-gold; either end can go first.
part_guide.led_yellow: The yellow round LED warns before red. Its long leg is the anode (+); its short leg beside the flat rim is the cathode (-).
part_guide.res_yellow: This banded 220 ohm resistor limits the yellow LED's current. It has no positive or negative end.
part_guide.led_green: The green round LED shows the normal traffic-go state. Its long leg is the anode (+); its short leg beside the flat rim is the cathode (-).
part_guide.res_green: This banded 220 ohm resistor limits the green LED's current. It has no positive or negative end.
part_guide.button: The square 12 mm button has four metal legs and a central plunger. Pressing it connects D2 to ground; the Arduino's internal pull-up keeps D2 HIGH when released.
part_guide.wire_ground: The black wire from an Uno GND header to the first top-edge ground-rail hole establishes shared ground.
part_guide.wire_red_signal: The red wire connects the Uno header labelled 11 to the red LED's anode row.
part_guide.wire_red_ground: This black wire runs from row 15 up to the ground rail, completing the red LED's path through its resistor.
part_guide.wire_yellow_signal: The yellow wire connects the Uno header labelled 10 to the yellow LED's anode row.
part_guide.wire_yellow_ground: This black wire runs from row 25 up to the ground rail, completing the yellow LED's path through its resistor.
part_guide.wire_green_signal: The green wire connects the Uno header labelled 9 to the green LED's anode row.
part_guide.wire_green_ground: This black wire runs from row 35 up to the ground rail, completing the green LED's path through its resistor.
part_guide.wire_button_signal: The blue wire connects the Uno header labelled 2 to the button's row 44 contact.
part_guide.wire_button_ground: This black wire grounds the button's row 46 contact, so a press sends a LOW signal to D2.

tests.title: Test the red LED
tests.what_it_tests: Checks the red LED, its resistor, the D11 connection, and the shared ground connection.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The red LED should blink repeatedly: half a second on, then half a second off. Unplug the USB cable before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Re-check step 3: the red LED's long leg belongs in 10e and its short leg in 11e. Check the resistor in step 4 at 11d and 15d, the D11 jumper in step 11 at 10a, and the ground jumper in step 12 at 15a and the top negative rail next to row 15. Check step 10 connects Uno GND to the same negative rail next to row 1.

tests.title: Test the yellow LED
tests.what_it_tests: Checks the yellow LED, its resistor, and its D10-to-ground circuit.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The yellow LED should blink repeatedly: half a second on, then half a second off. The red LED should stay off. Unplug the USB cable before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Re-check step 5: the yellow LED's long leg belongs in 20e and its short leg in 21e. Check step 6's resistor at 21d and 25d, step 13's jumper from D10 to 20a, and step 14's ground jumper from 25a to the top negative rail next to row 25. Check step 10's Uno GND connection and that the rail is continuous between rows 1 and 25.

tests.title: Test all three lights
tests.what_it_tests: Checks the green LED circuit and confirms that D11, D10, and D9 control the correct lights independently.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Only one LED should light at a time: red for one second, yellow for one second, then green for one second, repeating. The button is not connected yet and has no effect. Unplug the USB cable before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: For green, re-check step 7's LED legs at 30e (long) and 31e (short), step 8's resistor at 31d and 35d, step 15's D9 jumper to 30a, and step 16's ground jumper from 35a to the negative rail next to row 35. If green alone fails, check whether that rail has a break between step 10's GND connection near row 1 and row 35. For red or yellow problems, re-check steps 3–4 and 11–12, or steps 5–6 and 13–14, respectively.

assumptions: No existing bench placement was provided, so this is a fresh layout.
The outer rail above column a is the ground (-) rail along the top edge. No positive power rail is used.
The specified rail is continuous along all 63 rows, as required by this breadboard model.
View the breadboard with its long axis vertical and row 1 at the top to see red, yellow and green in a traffic-light column. Top-edge ground-rail wording refers to the unrotated model.

The button has four legs: the across-body pair in row 44 is permanently connected, the across-body pair in row 46 is permanently connected, and pressing joins the two rows. Across-body spacing is about 12.5 mm and same-side spacing about 5 mm.
LED leads are gently formed to fit adjacent rows without touching.
The Uno rendering uses the required 55 by 28 by 7 mm template, not the actual Uno Rev3 outline of 68.6 by 53.4 mm. Terminal anchor indices are symbolic; use printed header labels.
Resistor rendering dimensions are approximate; the exact connections are defined by their mounting holes.
The three required resistors are in the LEDs' cathode return paths, following the specified wiring pattern; a series resistor limits current on either side of an LED.
Jumper colours identify their roles; use matching colours where available.

plan.final_result: The LEDs form one evenly spaced line: red at row 10, yellow at row 20 and green at row 30. With row 1 facing upward, they appear in a vertical traffic-light column. Once the sketch is loaded and USB power is present, only green lights initially. A button press gives 2 seconds of yellow, then 5 seconds of red as the crossing cue, then green again. Presses during a cycle are ignored; release and press again after green returns to request another cycle.
safety: Keep the Uno disconnected from USB and other power while inserting or changing components.
Use USB power for this project; do not connect mains electricity or a 12 V supply to breadboard holes or Arduino GPIO pins.
Each LED must retain its own 220 ohm series resistor. Never replace a resistor with a jumper.
Keep exposed LED and resistor leads from touching adjacent leads, and never force the button into incompatible holes.
The button needs no external pull-up resistor because the sketch enables INPUT_PULLUP. Do not connect the button to 5 V.
This is a tabletop demonstration, not a real road or pedestrian safety controller.
